I've barbacked at my bar (country bar) for about 2 years now and have recently been pushed to learn bartending by management. I've been honestly reluctant about jumping in head first for awhile but I've been picking up slower day shifts here and there. It's definitely better money than barbacking and at least as far as physically, it's way easier. My dilemma is that for a plethora of different reasons, I haven't touched alcohol in over 10 years, in fact I've sworn myself from ever doing so (straight edge). I am not going to taste my drinks, so I assume I'll need to lean heavily on my count and memory of each mix drink. A couple of bartenders at the bar have been training me but I'm still so self concious about my situation. I definitely heard of a few people that don't drink at all and have been really successful bartending, so I know that it's not impossible. Does anyone have any advice for my situation?
Learning to bartend and not drinking at all yourself.

Now, I'm a firm believer that knowing how your drinks taste is fairly important. It's hard to describe what something tastes like, if you've never tasted it. A good part about Bartending though, is that it really is a science, as well as an art form. Most drinks out there have clearly marked instructions on how to create it, and I feel like it's safe to trust the recipe. You may wonder about variations on a popular drink, or creating a drink of your own, which is something Bartenders love to do. The only advice I can give to this point is that with enough experience, creating a drink based on your inherent knowledge of the alcohol (even without taste) is possible, especially if you're familiar with the non-alcoholic contents you're putting in the drink. I'm not going to say that you won't be limited by your inability to drink, but I will say that I think you have a shot, if you really devote yourself to the theories, and skills bartenders need to possess.

Hmmm. I would find this difficult to do... Let me explain.

There is a certain method to bartending. Ive been at it long enough that if a patron comes in wanting a drink they received at another bar (which happens often, strangely enough - I'll have people ask for some signature drink from who knows where) I can make it - as long as they know the ingredients. There are some basic building blocks to consider when preparing a cocktail and knowing the ratio of ingredients is integral (for ex. more liquor, less cordial, splash spritzer/ juice) and goes a long way in that type of situation. However, I would find it challenging to describe the citrus of a cocktail, the malt in a brown ale, or the hop characteristics of an IPA without having first hand knowledge of what I was serving. Knowledge is power in bartending.

I'm sure you could learn the lingo, but you would have to be very diligent as far as researching each and every beer, wine, and spirit. I think it's important to know exactly what you are serving and the easiest way is by tasting what you are serving beforehand. It's one thing to tell a patron a,b,c is aged in oak barrels because it's what you read through research and another to describe it as an experience of smokey, charred, or hint of oak because use you have tasted it personally. Obviously that is out of the question for you. So, I would be diligent in also researching what others have described tasting in a,b,c and not just the info from brewer/distillery/winery details and their descriptions.

I noticed your place bar is mentioned as a "country bar". What type of cocktails are you required to make? If your serving mostly bud heavys, jack and cokes, and Long Island iced teas I don't really see it as a huge issue. (Literally, I'm imagining a Dive)

Anyway, good luck in your bartending endeavors! If you have any questions, Hit me up.

I see what you mean about being able to accurately describe the characteristics of beers and such. Generally we've only got a couple of craft beers on tap/in the cooler. It's mostly bottled domestics like Bud Lights, Jack and coke, bombs like you mentioned. Nothing too fancy. We do have a drink menu and there's a couple of mixed drinks like a breakfast shot, raspberry mojito, johnny vegas. I've gotten most of those down but I've only been working day shifts, I feel like the second I get working a night shift it'll be a different story and I'll need to depend heavily on the elements of cocktails foreign to me like you mentioned. I've just been concentrating on my count as much as I can, doing as many single liquor drinks as I can. Thanks for the advice for sure, If I get stuck with something and I'm to embarrassed to ask a coworker, I'll definitely be hitting you up lol.
